title: Before Abraham was (John 8:58)
hook: before Abraham was made, I am

segments.voice: Yesterday, the whole sentence: if you continue in my word, the truth shall make you free. Your line was the truth sets free.

Before my grandmother was born, I am. A grammar teacher would circle that in red. The tenses don't match; it should be I was. Nobody says it this way. And yet that's the sentence at the end of John chapter eight, and the wrong tense is the point. The argument in the temple has been going on a long time, and getting hotter. It's about Abraham, the father of the people. And Jesus ends it with two words that make his listeners reach for stones.
screen: `A SENTENCE WITH THE WRONG TENSE.` → `AN ARGUMENT ABOUT ABRAHAM.` → `TWO WORDS, AND STONES.`

segments.voice: Jesus says that Abraham rejoiced to see his day; he saw it and was glad. His listeners answer, reasonably: you're not yet fifty years old, and you've seen Abraham? And he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Amen, amen I say to you, before Abraham was made, I am." Listen to the two verbs. Abraham was made: he came into being at a point in time, like all of us. I am: not I was, not I came to be. Just is. The Church hears in it: no beginning. Why the stones? Readers connect it to a name. At the burning bush, Moses asked God's name, and the Douay-Rheims gives the answer: "I AM WHO AM." A man saying I am like that could be heard as claiming the name of God, which to a devout listener would be blasphemy. John doesn't spell out their reason. They take up stones; he hides himself and goes out of the temple. We met the Word who was in the beginning on the first day of this Gospel. This is the same claim, now in his own mouth. The Catholic Church reads it plainly: the Son is eternal, one in being with the Father, God from God. It's in the Creed every Sunday: begotten, not made. And the argument here isn't between Christians and Jews as we know them now. It's among Jewish people in the temple, with a Jewish teacher, over what God had revealed. The Church teaches that this conflict must never be used to blame the Jewish people as a whole.
screen: `ABRAHAM WAS MADE.` · `I AM: NO BEGINNING.` · `I AM WHO AM, AT THE BUSH.` · `BEGOTTEN, NOT MADE.` · then, large: `BEFORE ABRAHAM WAS MADE, I AM.`

segments.voice: On the in-breath, say silently, I; on the out-breath, am, slowly, again and again, adding nothing after it, not tired, not late, just I am. If you pray, hold the words as God's name, given at the bush and spoken in the temple; if not, rest in the plain fact of being here.
Ego eimi. The Greek for I am, which Jesus said of himself before Abraham was ever made, echoing God's name at the burning bush. Today's word.
Your line: I am. Two short words, and no beginning at all. That's day five hundred nine.

howItsDone: Catholics profess in the Nicene Creed at Sunday Mass that the Son is "begotten, not made," and hear John 8:51–59 at a weekday Mass in the fifth week of Lent.

original.note: Greek: I am (John 8:58), set against Abraham's genesthai, came to be.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus was claiming to be very old.
what it means: the Church reads it as a claim to exist without beginning, in words that echo God's own name.
what a scholar hears: genesthai (came to be) for Abraham, eimi (am) for himself; the Greek Old Testament renders Exodus 3:14 with egō eimi.

chat.says: Why did people pick up stones when Jesus said "before Abraham was made, I am"?
options: Readers hear God's name from the burning bush in it; it could sound like blasphemy.
They thought he was lying about his age, since he was not yet fifty years old.
He had insulted Abraham, saying Abraham was never glad to see his day.
chat.meaning: I am echoes God's answer at the bush, I AM WHO AM. John doesn't spell out their reason, but readers connect the stones to that name.

notes: Confirm the Douay's capitalization of John 8:58 (some printings read 'I AM'); the validator compares case-insensitively.

Blasphemy framing and the stones (8:59): the script presents the listeners' reaction as understandable from their own faith, and cites Nostra Aetate 4 and CCC 597 against collective blame. Confirm the framing.
LXX Exodus 3:14 reads 'egō eimi ho ōn'; stated as 'renders Exodus 3:14 with egō eimi'. Confirm.
